questions.prompt: The Wikipedia article "Development of Duke Nukem Forever" chronicles fourteen years of stalled production, four complete engine overhauls, and a lawsuit, including a moment when a blunt, profanity-filled email was fired off in frustration at a company pressing for progress updates. Which company was on the receiving end of that profane message from a 3D Realms co-founder?
questions.hint: It was neither the engine maker (Epic Games) nor a company known mainly for unrelated franchises (Activision).
questions.explanation: The publisher Take-Two Interactive, which was funding the project and demanding milestone reports, received a profanity-laden response from 3D Realms co-founder George Broussard amid the escalating dispute that eventually led to a lawsuit and 3D Realms' shutdown.

questions.prompt:
Which unusual article does the following describe?

This article catalogs the vast array of merchandise and spin-off media generated by a long-running animated television franchise. It covers categories such as video games, comic books, trading cards, toys, clothing, a theme park ride, and even a feature film, reflecting how deeply the show's characters and imagery have been licensed across consumer products over several decades.
questions.hint: The franchise highlighted here began airing after 1980, which rules out Looney Tunes and Scooby-Doo, as both originated several decades earlier.
questions.explanation: The article details the extensive merchandise line stemming from The Simpsons, including video games, comics, toys, and other licensed products tied to the animated series.

questions.prompt: The Wikipedia article "Halifax Slasher" describes a 1938 panic in Halifax, England, over a mysterious attacker who turned out never to have existed, as the supposed victims had actually wounded themselves. When two men eventually confessed to faking their injuries and causing public mischief, what punishment did a court hand down to them?
questions.hint: The sentence went beyond a simple verbal warning, and it was not limited to supervised community-based correction.
questions.explanation: The two men who admitted to faking their slashing injuries were sentenced to twelve months of hard labor for causing public mischief.

questions.prompt: The Wikipedia article "Cargo cult" describes rituals that tribal groups developed hoping to attract the wealth and goods of more technologically advanced societies. One such movement on the Pacific island of Tanna, in Vanuatu, went so far as to revere a living member of the British royal family as a divine ancestral spirit. Which royal figure was worshipped in this way?
questions.hint: The figure was male and never reigned as monarch himself.
questions.explanation: The Prince Philip Movement on Tanna island in Vanuatu revered Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, as a divine figure, believing he was a pale-skinned son of a mountain spirit destined to marry a powerful woman (Queen Elizabeth II) overseas.

questions.prompt: This bronze equestrian monument to a 19th century military commander and statesman stands outside a major city art gallery in the United Kingdom. Although it is a protected heritage structure, it has become internationally famous for an ongoing act of informal decoration added by local residents, which the city council has repeatedly removed but which keeps reappearing. The decoration has become such a beloved symbol of the city that attempts to legally prevent it were abandoned, and it has even been referenced in official tourism material.
choices: Equestrian statue of the Duke of Wellington, Glasgow
Equestrian statue of Richard the Lionheart, London
Equestrian statue of King William III, Glasgow
Equestrian statue of Prince Albert, Edinburgh
questions.hint: The correct answer is located in Glasgow, not in London or Edinburgh.

article.title: Equestrian statue of the Duke of Wellington, Glasgow

questions.explanation: The statue depicts the Duke of Wellington outside the Gallery of Modern Art in Glasgow, and is famous for almost always having a traffic cone placed on its head, a tradition the city has come to embrace as a cultural icon.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a real unusual Japanese television program that paired stretching and gymnastic routines with teaching 'useful' English phrases such as 'Spare me my life!', 'I am allergic to penicillin', and 'I have a bad case of diarrhea'?
questions.hint: The real program's title is not 'Genki English Gym' or 'Muscle Talk English Hour', those are invented names that don't match the actual Japanese broadcast.
questions.explanation: Zuiikin' English was a Japanese TV show that combined gymnastic exercises with lessons on practical, often absurd English phrases.

questions.prompt: The Wikipedia article "Crime in Antarctica" shows that the frozen continent isn't quite as lawless as the Wild West, but it has seen its share of shocking incidents. One of the most infamous involved a Soviet researcher in 1959 who attacked and killed a colleague after a heated disagreement over a tabletop pastime, leading Soviet authorities to ban the activity at their Antarctic stations entirely. What was this banned game?
questions.hint: It's not a game played with tiles, and it doesn't involve a standard 52-card deck.
questions.explanation: After a Soviet scientist killed a colleague in a dispute during a chess match at a Soviet Antarctic station in 1959, chess was reportedly banned at Soviet Antarctic research stations.

questions.prompt:
This Wikipedia article describes a series of areas that were designated off-limits after a major early 20th-century war, because the land was so devastated by shelling, unexploded munitions, and chemical residue that it was deemed unfit for human habitation. More than a century later, some of these zones remain fenced off and uninhabited, with ongoing efforts to clear buried arsenic, lead, and unexploded shells still underway. A few sections have gradually been reopened for limited forestry or agriculture after extensive decontamination work.

Where is the topic of this unusual article located?
questions.hint: This is not in Africa, not in Asia, and not in North America.
questions.explanation: The Zone rouge refers to areas of France devastated and contaminated after World War I, some of which remain uninhabited to this day.

questions.prompt:
Which unusual article does the following describe?

This is a question in geometry that asks for the shape of the largest possible area that can be carried, while remaining rigid, around a right-angled corner in a hallway of unit width. Although the problem is simple to state and visualize, finding the exact optimal shape has proven extremely difficult, and mathematicians have spent decades proposing candidate shapes and narrowing down upper and lower bounds without reaching a definitive solution.
questions.hint: The answer has nothing to do with runners racing around a track, and it does not involve squares inscribed inside curves.
questions.explanation: The article describes the moving sofa problem, a famous unsolved problem in mathematics that seeks the largest area shape that can be maneuvered around a right-angle turn in a corridor of unit width.

questions.prompt:
Which unusual article does the following describe?

This is a yearly event, first held in 2006, in which participants around the world are encouraged to perform a particular private act at the same moment (timed to the winter solstice) in hopes that the resulting surge of energy would help bring about world peace. It was organized by a pair of activists and received widespread media attention for its unconventional approach to promoting peace.
choices: The Annual Global Orgasm for Peace
questions.hint: The correct event does not involve staying quiet, and it is not centered on meditation.

article.title: The Annual Global Orgasm for Peace

questions.explanation: The Annual Global Orgasm for Peace is an event, begun in 2006, that calls on people worldwide to have an orgasm simultaneously at the winter solstice, with organizers claiming the collective energy released could promote world peace.
